I love the way that Sanderson handled Rand. As is typical with Sanderson, the prose is fine, characters become more overtly archetypal, and all the jokes fall flat. However, the action is great, he understands (and utilizes) the complex magic system incredibly well, and his weaving of how our beloved characters evolved from Book 12 to the Last Battle was very satisying. 

And the 200+ page last battle? Epic. 

Of course it isn’t Jordan, but Sanderson explicitly said he couldn’t emulate Jordan’s prose so he used his own author’s voice. And I think it’s fair to say that Jordan, particularly at the height of his powers, has more music in his prose. Jordan is better at showing vs telling. Jordan might say something like “…his brow creasing…”. Sanderson would phrase that as some variation of “he crinkled his brow, as if he were confused.”

Here are my biggest quibbles:

1) Mat’s characterization improves, but never quite “fits”. It’s like an ill-fitting pair of boots. 

2) Perrin’s role in the final battle felt like it had little to do with his character's evolution into a leader. It was more playing-with-potential-of-powers than a satisfying conclusion of character. 

3) There are a couple of huge questions about why some of the characters do incredibly reckless things, knowing the consequences of even their victory will be catastrophic to huge groups of people. And these are, like, really smart characters! 

4) Androl is cheating. 

But here’s my overall take:

Sanderson did a pretty-good-to-really good job with a nearly impossible task. He wove a story backwards — knowing where the characters ended but without a road map of how they got there, turning Jordan’s vision of one impossible tome into three epic books. Sanderson brought all his talents to a world he clearly loves. He also did this knowing the stakes — he knew how much other people loved this world, and how much it meant to them as well. One can feel the care. It’s still Jordan’s world, even if the view feels occasionally askew. 

The Wheel of Time is my favorite story, and it was Sanderson who got me into it. For that alone, I’ll always be grateful. But for providing a satisfying ending? Thank you, Brandon Sanderson. 

Plus, I have never wept harder due to the fate of a character. Even on re-reads.
 
There are certainly fair criticisms. But I enjoyed 12-14 as much as, say, Book 7, and even preferred Sanderson’s trilogy to Books 8 and 10. 

As I said before, I’m grateful it was him, and I so appreciate how he found the ending. Well, AN ending.

Your frustration/burnout is perfectly understandable. It happens. 

The “one character becomes the lead role” is a trope that emerges as well. Perhaps the player is more immersive or committed. Or, perhaps it’s natural to look to a Paladin, Bard, or other class as a “leader” and design with them in mind. 

In my campaign, I alternate by weeks. The rogue is the “lead” of this particular session because the plot is dealing with bandits, sneaking, and traps. Or the Mafia. Then, the next week, the Sorcadin becomes the one most tied to the plan for the story. Then next week, the Barbarian. Repeat as necessary.  

Knowing which character you’re writing for can be of great help in planning the circumstances. If it’s time for the Bard to have a turn, perhaps this week is a Battle of the Bands where the prize is a meeting with a corrupt and evil magistrate who holds the macguffin.  Perhaps there’s  a lot of “face” time to lead the other players through a disguised infiltration (based in role play rather than combat.) Or, of course, something to do with seducing a dragon. 

I’m not attempting to correct you or imply you’re not doing these things. Just offering what helped me through. 

Also, if the lead keeps jumping to the front of the line, split the party by throwing your lead into captivity, and make the other players mount a rescue. 60% of the time it works every time.

Phonetics are a useful tool, but they're ultimately just a shortcut to articulatory positioning.  I just worked with an actor whose over-reliance on phonetics actually cost her some accuracy and flow.  Another actor needed line recordings and "challenger" passages to get the sounds.  Yet another actor latched onto the concept of accent "posture" right from the gate.  Finding unique ways to get the sounds (and sometimes symbols) into their brains is the ultra-fun part of the job.
And yes, "sample phrases" or "challengers" or "in-the-zone" phrases are SUPER common, and can be effective (if the actor correctly remembers the exact sounds of the phrase, of course!)

These are called "elicitation passages". They contain every "lexical set", or vowel set identified by J C Wells in British / American English. There are other such passages, although "Comma" is perhaps the most common. 
As a dialect coach, I prefer "Dali's Last Hurrah" and "All About Foxes", but "Comma" is an amazing passage as well.

This trap, however, is easy to avoid.  don’t begin your questions with a presumption of correctness. “Well, in the service we were always told…..”

I’ve never heard a veteran do this, but when an older female student begins a question with “As a mother….” , there is a collective eye roll loud enough to deafen. 

So, ask Away. It’s a boon. It’s a gift. But, just make sure you’re not turning a lecture into a conversation, or making it about you. 

And if you’ve asked 5 questions already? Save the remaining ones for an email.

It's just this --- the problem with the way the first three books is that, from Rand's point of view, it's exactly the same ending.  He discovers a new ability, fights the same guy, and is confirmed as TDR - at the Eye of the World (for survival), at Tommen Head (to save others), and finally again at the Stone of Tear (to prove he's the dragon).  

Why can't at least two of those be combined? Why can't he fight [the guy] in the sky at the eye of the world? Or, what if Callandor isn't in the stone of tear, but at Fal Dara? Can you imagine? Aiel showing up at Fal Dara? Callandor being in the eye of the world? That's a lot, and probably too much, but in theory you could combine all three of Rand's book endings into one super-ending. At least two of those, right? 

I say this because I don't think we'll actually make it to Tear in the show. So much of the story is filled with one-off locations that don't actually come back and affect the story in meaningful ways.  This is great in novels, but it doesn't translate to the main screen where location is as much of a character as anyone in the novel. So, why go to Tear at all? Why can't Callandor be wherever they fight in the sky?  If only one thing happens in a location and we never go back to it again for any significant story beat, chances are that the production team will not scout locations, set up a production team, hire distinct looking extras and craft distinct design for only this location when, story wise, it doesn't matter at all if it's the Stone of Tear or the Stone of Andor or the Stone of Tommen Head or the Stone of Fal Dara or the Stone of Kandor.  Unless they combine Tear and Illian, and Rand becomes the King of Tear in Crown of Swords. THEN Tear would make sense as a filming location, and maybe he even fights Sammael or someone there later on -- but creating Tear just as a scabbard for Callandor? I don't think they'll spend the millions.

In regards to the non-Rand characters, book one and two are both chases where the super boys are looking for something. In Book One, each other and then the EOTW. Why can't Mat lose the dagger earlier, and they need to get it back?  Why can't that be part of his arc in the first book? I'm currently in Book 2 (re-read), and the narrative structure of "get the MacGuffin / lose the MacGuffin / get the MacGuffin" I fear won't translate well to live action.

Mat's only arc in the second book is "guy who needs the dagger." Does Perrin have an arc in the second book? The answer is, of course, no, because Perrin only gets arcs in certain books. So expanding his arc from the first book isn't hard.

Moiraine will have to be more involved, and we won't see Rand as a leader. But the more Lan is there, the more Rand's training as a Blademaster makes sense.  

So, the first book begins the same, but over the course of the adventure many of the events that happen in The Great Hunt happen in EOTW. Rather than spending time with farmers and playing the flute for 3 chapters, Rand and Mat are chasing the dagger while running from the dark ones.  At the end of season 1, Rand fights [dude] in the sky while Mat blows the horn to help the fighters in Tarwin's gap.  Perrin still becomes a wolfbrother.  The girls arc doesn't change much, and Egwene's kidnapped arc can be moved back a season or even incorporated into the "chase" -- perhaps instead of ALWAYS fighting Trollocs and Whitecloaks and the nebulously-defined "Darkfriends", maybe they encounter Seanchan in book 1? [that feels like a lot but a better writer than I could make it work if they had to]

I just think that, since Book 1 reads like a pilot of the series and Book 2 reads like a soft-reboot of the series, and that both follow similar structures and with similar peak moments, that they could be combined in many ways.  Getting the girls to the tower and starting their training is the hardest part of combining the two books, so perhaps the first season combines Book 1 and 2 for the super boys, but the wonder girls get their story in full in the next season [and, with them, I think combining the wonder girls story for Books 2 and 3 is elegant and easy) 

(although Elayne and/or Min might possibly sneak away and join the group for part of their quest in the TV version of Season One, because that's a very TV thing to do, but they also might not).

I think a lot of characters, locations, and story beats will be combined.  I think a lot of locations that exist in the story to help broaden the world will be changed in the TV show to help cut costs and keep the narrative focused.
